Graduate Student Loan Performance and Implications for the New Federal Lending Limits 
 Discussion Paper
 Graduate Student Loan Performance and Implications for the New Federal Lending Limits
 by
 Jordan Matsudaira , 
 Tomás E. Monarrez  & 
 Dubravka Ritter 
 November 2026
 DP 26-03 – This report examines the historical performance of federal graduate student borrowers and its implications for the new federal lending limits for graduate borrowers.
 View PDF
 Share
 Combining enrollment records with credit bureau data and program-level earnings, we measure three-year default among federal graduate borrowers who entered repayment between 2011 and 2016. Students whose borrowing exceeded the new limits defaulted more often than others, but loan size alone is a coarse signal of repayment risk. Pre-enrollment credit scores are the strongest predictor of default among the factors we examine, followed by the credential pursued and the median earnings of a program’s past graduates. Among borrowers with low or no credit scores, who are unlikely to qualify for traditional private loans, those in high-earning programs default at far lower rates than those in lower-earning ones. These patterns suggest that information on program outcomes, considered alongside credit history, may help identify lower-risk borrowers among students whose credit records alone would limit their access to private credit.
